title: Punctuating Clauses
keyIdea: An independent clause has a subject and a verb and makes sense on its own. To join two of them in one sentence, mark the boundary with a semi-colon (two related clauses of equal weight), a colon (the second clause explains or expands the first) or a dash (the same job, less formal). Never use a comma alone: that is a comma splice. Test it by covering each side: both must stand alone.
familyTip: Pick two short sentences from a book, such as 'It was dark. We lit a candle.' Ask your child to join them three ways: with a semi-colon, with a colon if the second part explains the first, and with a dash for a story voice. Then try the cover test: hide one side with a finger and check the other still makes sense.

visual.caption: Which mark fits between the clauses? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: The match was off: the pitch was flooded.
I had one wish: a dog.
Lions hunt by night; zebras graze by day.
She was soaked: she had walked home in the rain.
The red team won; the blue team came second.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: sort clauses, mark the boundary in run-on sentences, choose colon or semi-colon, use the cover test, and fix a comma splice.

kid: A clause has a subject and a verb. An independent clause also makes sense on its own: 'The bus was late.' A part like 'because it snowed' does not. It leaves you waiting for more.
You can join two independent clauses into one sentence. Mark the boundary with a semi-colon when the clauses are linked and equal: 'Tom likes tea; Ana likes coffee.'

Use a colon when the second clause explains or adds detail to the first: 'I knew she was home: her bike was by the door.' A dash does the same job in a chatty story or diary: 'I opened the box – it was empty.'

Do not join two clauses with only a comma. 'It was cold, we wore coats' is a comma splice. Fix it with a semi-colon, a full stop, or a comma plus a word like so. Check by covering each side of the mark. Both sides must stand alone.
adult: Ages 10 to 11. This is Year 6 in the English National Curriculum, Appendix 2: the use of the semi-colon, colon and dash to mark the boundary between independent clauses, with the example 'It's raining; I'm fed up'. The KS2 grammar, punctuation and spelling test asks pupils to insert, choose and explain these marks. Key words: clause, independent clause, subordinate clause, boundary, semi-colon, colon, dash, comma splice.

Each mark has a job. A semi-colon links two closely related clauses of equal weight, often a balance or contrast. A colon points forward: the second clause explains, gives a reason for, or expands the first. A dash can stand in for either in informal writing and adds a sharper pause. All three need a full clause on both sides when they mark this boundary. Colons and semi-colons also have list uses, which are taught separately.

Common mistakes: the comma splice, joining two clauses with a comma alone; putting a semi-colon in front of a subordinate clause or phrase, as in 'I was tired; because I ran'; keeping the joining word as well, as in 'It rained; and we stayed in'; using a colon for two balanced clauses that do not explain each other; and over-using dashes in formal writing. Be careful with capitals: in British English the clause after a colon or semi-colon starts with a small letter.

In the lab your child sorts word groups into those that stand alone and those that cannot, taps where the first clause ends in three run-on sentences and chooses the mark, sorts sentences into colon or semi-colon, judges six marked sentences with the cover test, and picks every fix for a comma splice.

practice.prompt: You check {a} sentences with the cover test. {b} of them have a side that cannot stand alone. How many pass the test?
practice.hint: Take the sentences that fail away from all {a}.
practice.explain: {a} take away {b} leaves {=a-b} sentences where both sides stand alone.

practice.prompt: A paragraph has {a} comma splices. You fix each one with a semi-colon and also fix {b} fragments with full stops. How many marks did you change?
practice.hint: Count one change for each splice and one for each fragment.

choices: The bell rang; we went inside.
The bell rang, we went inside.
The bell rang; and we went inside.
practice.hint: Cover each side of the mark. Is there a joining word too?
practice.explain: 'The bell rang' and 'we went inside' both stand alone, so a semi-colon joins them. A comma alone is a splice, and a semi-colon does not need 'and'.

practice.prompt: Which mark fits? 'The trip was cancelled __ the coach had broken down.'
choices: A colon, because the second part explains the first
A comma, because it is a short pause
No mark at all
practice.hint: Does the second clause tell you why?
practice.explain: The second clause gives the reason, so a colon fits. A comma alone would be a comma splice.

practice.prompt: What is wrong with 'After the film; we had pizza.'?
choices: 'After the film' cannot stand alone
Nothing is wrong
It needs a dash instead
practice.hint: Cover the part after the semi-colon. Does the first part make sense alone?
practice.explain: 'After the film' is a phrase, not an independent clause. Use a comma: After the film, we had pizza.

choices: The dog barked
When the dog barked
Barking at the door
pool.hint: Which one makes sense on its own?
pool.explain: 'The dog barked' has a subject and a verb and stands alone. The others leave you waiting for more.

pool.prompt: Which mark shows the second clause explains the first?
choices: A colon
A semi-colon
A comma
pool.hint: Which mark points forward to an explanation?
pool.explain: A colon says: here is what I mean. A semi-colon links two equal clauses.

pool.prompt: 'Owls hunt at night __ hawks hunt by day.' Which mark fits best?
choices: A semi-colon
A colon
A comma
pool.hint: Do the two clauses explain each other, or balance each other?
pool.explain: The two clauses are a balanced contrast, so a semi-colon fits. A comma alone would be a splice.

pool.prompt: Which fixes the comma splice 'It was late, we went home.'?
choices: It was late; we went home.
It was late we went home.
It was late, and, we went home.
pool.hint: A comma alone cannot join two clauses.
pool.explain: A semi-colon joins the two clauses. With no mark it is a run-on; extra commas round 'and' are wrong.

pool.prompt: Where does a dash between clauses fit best?
choices: In a diary: I looked up – the kite had gone.
In a list: pens – rulers – glue
After a phrase: In the morning – we left.
pool.hint: A dash between clauses needs a full clause on each side.
pool.explain: In informal writing a dash can mark the boundary between two clauses. It does not separate list items or follow a phrase.

pool.prompt: Which sentence uses a semi-colon wrongly?
choices: I stayed in; because it rained.
I stayed in; it rained all day.
Sam ran; Jo walked.
pool.hint: Cover each side. Which one has a side that cannot stand alone?
pool.explain: 'Because it rained' cannot stand alone, so the semi-colon is wrong. Drop it: I stayed in because it rained.

pool.prompt: You join {a} pairs of clauses with semi-colons and {b} pairs with colons. How many marks is that?
pool.hint: Each joined pair has one mark at its boundary.

pool.prompt: A story has {a} sentences joined by commas alone. Each one is a comma splice to fix. If you fix 2 with full stops, how many are left to fix?
pool.hint: Start with {a} splices and take away the 2 you fixed.
pool.explain: {a} take away 2 leaves {=a-2} comma splices to fix with a semi-colon, colon or dash.

choices: Hide each side of the mark and check it stands alone
Count the words on each side
Read it out loud fast
pool.hint: What must be true of both sides?
pool.explain: Both sides of a semi-colon, colon or dash between clauses must be independent clauses, so cover each side in turn and check.
